The Enemy in the Mirror: India as a Disguise
The Origin of the Aryan Invasion Theory
Ghosts in the Academy: Modern Textbooks

blocks.text: A British collector in Madurai would dismount near goddess Meenakshi's temple and walk barefoot past her shrine. Another baits in Ganga every morning and proudly calls himself a convert. Britain's greatest scholar declared Sanskrit finer than both Greek and Latin, praising Indian astronomy  and medicine. But within a single generation, it was all gone. >>  >> The same empire that once admired India was now calling Hindus savages and their

gods monsters.  So, what changed? To answer that, we have to understand one book written by one man. Because for next two centuries, his ideas would not only shape how Britain saw India, but how Indians came to see themselves. James Mill's impact on India was extraordinary, but the story before him might be even more unbelievable. During the late 18th century, many East India Company officials admired Indian civilization. Company officials

patronized temples and mosques. Government offices closed on Indian festivals. Christian missionaries were often prevented from aggressively converting Hindus. Some British scholars believed India possessed one of the oldest and most sophisticated civilization in the world. Historians even have a name for this period, Indomania. So, if Britain already admired India, how did it end up believing in the exact opposite? The answer begins after the defeat of the Marathas. >>  >> Once the East India Company transformed

from a trading corporation into an empire, admiration becomes a problem. See, if Indians possessed an ancient and sophisticated civilization, how could Britain justify ruling them? The empire needed a moral argument. The gulf between ruler and ruled had to be widened. If evidence for Indian backwardness didn't exist, it had to be manufactured. And no one supplied that justification more successfully than James Mill.

James Mill was a son of Scottish shoemaker, poor, brilliant, ambitious, and terrified of remaining poor. He failed to secure a position in the church and moved to London scraping by as a struggling writer. But, writing paid poorly, and with large family to support, Mill needed something bigger. The richest corporation at the time was the East India Company. So, Mill decided to write what he hoped would become the definitive history of India. There was only one problem. He had never been to India. He never  learned Sanskrit, Persian, or any Indian

language. He never met the people he was describing. James Mill argued that this actually made him more objective. Instead, he relied heavily on missionary writings, accounts dripping with alarm and moral outrage, where India was portrayed as a land lost in darkness. Its temples described as dens of adultery, and its gods condemned as demons in disguise. When book appeared in 1817, it transformed his life. The company rewarded him with a lucrative senior post. The country he attacked in

print was now signing his paycheck. What happened next is what made his book so dangerous. The company adopted his book as required reading for future civil servants traveling to India. Mill's ideas helped shift the mindset of company officials from admiration to deep suspicion and contempt. They provided intellectual cover for harsher treatment of ordinary Indians, influenced policies that contributed to devastating famines, and justified efforts to replace India's own languages with English. A private opinion had

quietly become a state policy. And as you will see, that the story didn't end with British Empire. In many ways, we are still living with its consequences. But, who did James Mill really hate? Surprisingly, it wasn't India. It was Britain. Mill belonged to the utilitarian movement, a group of political reformers who believed Britain's traditional institutions were corrupt and stood in the way of progress. Their biggest targets were monarchy, the aristocracy,

and especially the Church of England. But openly attacking these institutions invited trouble. India offered a safer target, and once you see that, a remarkable pattern emerges. Again and again, Mill takes the very institutions he despised in Britain and projects them onto India. Let's test that claim. James Mill portrayed Brahmins as the wealthy priestly corporation manipulating religion for profit. But India had no pope, no centralized church, and no compulsory religious taxation. Most

village Brahmins lived in poverty. The institution Mill was actually describing looked far more like Church of England. The Anglican Church collected a compulsory 10% tithe from every household. Bishops sat in Parliament, clergymen frequently held multiple offices while drawing large incomes and living like aristocrats in London. Mill took Britain's clerical corruption and projected it onto Hinduism. The greedy Brahmin in his book often looks suspiciously like an English bishop. But Mill didn't stop there.

>>  >> He also portrayed Brahmins as people controlling its laws, rulers, and society. That brings us to next parallel. Mill claimed that in Hindu system of governance, there are hardly any laws. And everything operated according to the arbitrary whims of the kings. The reality was almost opposite. The Indian kings were bound by Dharma. Daily life, trade, and local disputes were governed by independent merchant guilds known as  Shrenis and self-governing village Panchayats. In

fact, British administrator Sir Charles famously described Indian villages as little republics. Even a sitting Peshwa could be tried, prosecuted for a murder, and punished by his own chief justice. In other words, political authority in India was far more decentralized and constrained than Mill suggested. Ironically, legal system James Mill spent years attacking was Britain's own. As a utilitarian, he argued England's unwritten, judge-made common laws gave judges arbitrary and

tyrannical power  because laws were never properly codified. He took that frustration, pinned it onto India, and ignored a system that was arguably more structured than his own. The  pattern continues with kings themselves. In one chapter, Mill describes Hindu rulers as absolute despots. In the next, he portrays them as helpless puppets controlled by Brahmins. Both cannot be true, but the contradiction reveals something important. Mill needed Hindu kings to be tyrants because he wanted to attack British monarchy. He needed Brahmins to be greedy because he wanted

to attack the church. India was merely the stage on which Britain's domestic conflicts were fought. Mill dismissed traditional Hindu education as hierarchical and rigid, but contemporary British surveys proved reality was different. I made a full video on decentralized Indian education system before British dismantled it. Link is in description. The same pattern appears again in Mill's treatment of women. He described Hindu women as living in abject slavery. Yet, married women in Britain lived under coverture. They could not independently

own property, keep their wages, or enter contracts. Meanwhile, Hindu women possessed traditions such as stridhan, their own recognized property rights, and women composed sacred hymns in Rigveda. Mill knew these facts. They simply didn't fit his narrative. And then comes the detail that gives the whole game away. The supposedly neutral judge openly praised periods of Muslim rule over earlier Hindu governance when British investigations later reported that many Muslim administrators had imposed harsher taxation  than Hindu rulers, Mill dismissed those

findings as prejudice. By this point, the pattern is unmistakable. The evidence mattered only when it supported his conclusions. Perhaps the most influential legacy of James Mill's worldview was the Aryan invasion theory. His central assumption that Indians were incapable of creating a great civilization laid the foundation. If India had achieved remarkable advances in mathematics, philosophy, astronomy, architecture, and literature, then by his logic, someone else must have brought them. Later European scholars

increasingly proposed that a lighter-skinned, supposedly more civilized Aryan race entered India from outside and created its high culture. The theory solved a colonial problem. It allowed Europeans to admire India's achievements without admiring Indians. >>  >> Even as the invasion model itself came under increasing scrutiny, the underlying habit of thought survived. When India achieved something extraordinary, look first for an outside explanation. Credit the achievement elsewhere. Maybe an invader. Doubt the indigenous legacy. Does this pattern

sound familiar to you? It began with James Mill. At this point, you might be thinking, "Interesting history, but James Mill died almost two centuries ago." He did, but that's not where this story ends. It's where it begins because ideas don't disappear when people die. They spread. Within decades, Mill's assumptions had entered encyclopedias, universities, and educational systems. The Encyclopedia Britannica completely rewrote its article on India to reflect Mill's judgments. His ideas had become the new

normal. And if you think those ideas disappeared with British Empire, look at how India is still discussed today. When historian Irfan Habib argues that India did not exist as nation until foreign empires created it. He's using Mill's map. When Romila Thapar interprets Indian history primarily through a rigid Marxist lens of conflict and caste struggle, she's adhering to Mill's oppressor versus oppressed framework. Thapar furiously defends Aryan migration theory based on Mill's assumptions. When Audrey Truschke approaches India's

classical achievements, including the Gupta era, with skepticism remarkably similar to Mill's. Orwin Sheldon Pollock extends Mill's conflation of Hindu traditions with political despotism. Wendy Doniger or all those Western Indologists, the names are different, the vocabulary is politically sanitized, the explicit racism is gone, but the underlying framework survives. India's unity is questioned, its achievements are downplayed. >> That this discourse has been internalized in conscious and unconscious ways by the mainstream academicians to such

an extent, the moment you want to bring about a change in history, all kind of negative epithets will be slapped on you. Right-wing, Hindutva, revisionist, and so on and so forth. It happens in India, it happens everywhere. >> This is where history becomes personal. If you ever grow up feeling that your culture was backward, irrational, embarrassing, or something that constantly needed an apology, part of that feeling has a history. James Mill wrote a book that shaped colonial officials. Those officials shaped

schools, schools shaped textbooks, textbooks shaped generations. >> It's a very old Roman mantra that if you want to bring a culture or a people into subjugation, what you need to do is basically destroy their culture. And what was being done through these writings was that the culture was being destroyed. After independence, we did not critically examine this discourse, and the very fact that this discourse

got appropriated by the leftists, that it continues. >> When James Mill's voice became so familiar that many Indians mistook it for their own, George Orwell once wrote, "Who controls the past controls the future." The greatest theft of the empire was not merely land or wealth. It was a memory. It convinced a civilization to forget what it had been then handed back a diminished version of itself. Next time someone tells you what India was, ask yourself one question, "Whose voice am I really hearing?"
